Great article, I’ve been following this blog for years but have never commented before. I thought I’d share, as I have always felt that I have the perfect job for the younger mustachians out there looking for ways to challenge themselves in this vein while building wealth. An Interagency Hotshot Crew is a group of 20 wildland firefighters that travel across the western U.S., Alaska, and sometimes Canada to work on large wildfires. It is almost exclusively hard manual labor for long hours over difficult terrain and conditions. It will push most young folks past what they thought they were capable of, and a dedication to physical fitness is a requirement of the job. Spending months with the same group of like minded people doing difficult things with a sense of purpose builds strong comradery and incredible friendships. You get to see many of the most beautiful parts of the country, and experience the impressive power of the natural world. You are basically living for free half of the year, as your meals are provided and you sleep on the ground. I can still remember the first time I ate a low-grade steak over a campfire after working 16 hours, it was the most delicious meal I’ve ever had. “Hunger is the best seasoning”, as one of my crewmembers liked to put it. After a long season (1000 + hours of overtime), newer folks get the entire winter off. If you leverage your free time and fire checks wisely, you can drastically improve your situation while staying debt free. I was able to finish college, do some travelling, and build my house, all while saving money. It’s definitely not for everyone, and I don’t know if I would recommend it for a long career as the schedule doesn’t lend itself to a very balanced lifestyle. But for someone in their 20s looking to challenge themselves, I’ve always felt it is an amazing job.

Interesting conversation. One thing I didn’t see anyone mention is the fact that humans, like virtually all other mammals, are hard-wired to do as little as possible outside of the necessities (finding food, shelter, fornicating, fighting enemies) because energy expended on activities not related to those necessary for survival may just cost one their survival, at least in the “old days” of the jungle. The same evolutionary factors that make our bodies not want to shed fat or what to eat (sweet, not bitter) are in play when deciding whether to take the stairs or the escalator. It’s highly likely that without the default of lazy that most of what makes up civilization wouldn’t exist, since virtually everything we’ve ever invented beyond ensuring basic survival has been to reduce energy expenditure. Why walk when you can drive? Why forage when you can farm? ETC.

So the human animal has to consciously make the decision to do that which goes against his/her basic instincts.

A great book about it: “Exercised: The Science of Physical Activity, Rest and Health”, by Daniel E. Lieberman.

#8705. Scott Eastwood Is Still Seeking a Rush, Just at a Slower Pace

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

He still surfs. He still trains jiujitsu and Muay Thai. And the actor still lifts and still enjoys putting himself in situations that demand something from him physically.

What has changed at 40 is the way he prepares for all of it.

There was a time when Eastwood could train hard, wake up sore, and trust that his body would bounce back. Now, he is far more interested in staying mobile, pain-free, and ready for whatever he wants to do outside the gym.

Over the last five years, Eastwood says that shift has become increasingly intentional.

“Recovery is probably the biggest difference,” Eastwood told M&F. “I think I’d probably put it number one. I listen to my body more and take more care in my recovery than I ever did in my 20s or 30s.”

This doesn’t mean that he’s less serious about training, it just means Eastwood’s objective has evolved. Looking like a capable athlete has given way to a much more important goal: staying physically capable.

“Obviously I want to be strong, but I also want to be really flexible and limber and be able to react to whatever the world throws at you, where you’re not going to pull something or you’re not going to hurt yourself.”

Eastwood ,who’s latest film, Lucky Strike, is now streaming on Hulu, used to organize his gym work around the familiar bodybuilding split—chest, back, and different muscle groups on different days.

Now he prefers training that puts his entire body to work.

“I think [now I’m] just a little bit more focused on holistic workouts,” Eastwood said. “I’m far more focused now on my core, just because of body pain and how your body feels, and all the things that feel better, which kind of stem out from your core.”

When he isn’t working on a film, Eastwood says he typically lifts three or four times per week, splitting those sessions between gym and home workouts. He also tries to fit in Muay Thai or jiujitsu. Yoga has become a constant.

Eastwood says there isn’t a day that passes where he doesn’t do some version of it, often half an hour in the morning and another later in the day.

When he is filming, the expectations change.

A 6 a.m. call time might require a 5 a.m. gym session. Long production days can already be physically taxing, so those workouts become less about progress. It’s an evolution in the thinking that every training session needs to prove something. Eastwood still trains hard, but there isn’t much value now in forcing his body through movements that no longer feel worth the risk.

“You’re spending a lot of time on your feet, and it’s typically physical,” Eastwood said. “So you’re kind of just doing a little more maintenance when you’re working. You’re not getting the gains that you might get if you’re not working.”

The gym has never been the only testing grounds for Eastwood.

Surfing, martial arts, and hiking are still a part of his life, and each demands something slightly different from his body.

It’s a large part why strength alone no longer satisfies him.

“If I want to continue to do jiujitsu, and I want to do Muay Thai, and I want to continue to surf, I’ve got to take care of my body,” Eastwood says. “Which means strength, flexibility, and mobility. I’ve got to kind of do all these things, or my body is going to get trashed doing these sports.”

Those activities also provide him with feedback that a mirror will miss. A stiff body doesn’t perform well on a surfboard. Poor mobility isn’t less obvious when someone is trying to control you on a mat. Carrying unnecessary soreness into either activity can turn something meant to be enjoyable into a problem quickly.

Eastwood hasn’t lost his appetite for these passions that come with risk. However, age has made him more selective about which risks within those passions are worth taking.

That means foregoing chasing a massive surf or testing himself on the mat against whoever wants to go the hardest. When he was younger, these thoughts might have not even entered into his thinking.

Now, it’s more thoughtful. He still wants the challenge, to compete with himself, and to feel capable. These activities are just no longer a barometer for his toughness.

Ask him what physical quality matters more now than it did at 25, and the answer is an understandable one.

“Flexibility,” Eastwood says. “Flexibility and just not being in pain. If you can take care of your body where you’re not in pain all the time, that’s really valuable.”

One of the biggest shifts for Eastwood is the attention to recovery.

Yoga, sauna sessions, and Epsom salt baths have all been part of his routine for years, but sleep has become especially important as both his training and work demands have changed.

“Just getting a good night’s sleep, I value it so much more now,” Eastwood says.

10 to 15-hour set days require focus, energy, and often physical effort. Arriving not fully rested often produces immediate consequences.

“I can’t do the job that I do well and focus if I haven’t had a great night’s sleep,” he said.

His approach to nutrition is also uncomplicated. Eastwood says he follows a Mediterranean-style diet built around whole foods, including fish, red meat, grains, and plenty of vegetables. He also refuses to turn an occasional bag of chips or dessert into a moral crisis.

“I don’t make it some hard and fast rule that you have to do,” he says. “I just think those just get a little too rigid.”

His preference for simplicity also played a role in why Eastwood became a co-owner of North Performance.

Eastwood says longtime friend Mike Lucas shared the frustration of trying to travel while managing individual supplements. Both men wanted something easier to maintain without pretending a supplement could replace the fundamentals.

“You still have to work out. You have to get good sleep and have good recovery,” he says. “Having good supplements is just going to help those things. The basics are the basics. They don’t change regardless.”

When he is filming, Eastwood says North is part of his morning routine, but the rest of his priorities remain the same.

He still has to eat well. He still has to move. If the day is packed and there are only 25 minutes for himself, he’ll find somewhere to fit in exercise, yoga, or mobility work. Everything beyond that is what he calls “extra credit.”

It’s a simplicity that defines fitness at 40 for him.

Looking strong doesn’t mean anything if his back is aching or his body is too tight to do the things all of his training was meant to prepare him for.

The goal going into the next decade is simple: keep enough strength to be useful, maintain mobility to move well, and have enough durability to keep saying yes to the things he enjoys.

“I think fit is more how you feel and less aesthetic,” Eastwood said. “[Looking good] is great, but if you’re in pain because you’re not doing it correctly, then who gives a shit about what you look like?”

#8700. Science Finds that Dairy May Not Lead to Excess Fat as First Thought

For a long time, the public were cautioned against regular dairy food consumption, but a recent study from the University of Toronto, published by the Journal of Nutrition, appears to show that frequently delving into eggs, milk, and cheeses, could actually benefit your health and won’t make you fat. Here’s why.

In the ‘70s, a war on saturated fat consumption encouraged us to avoid products like whole milk, butter, and cheese because of the high levels that they contain. Then wellness culture in the new millennium further derailed the case for diary, citing inflammation, acne, and disrupted hormones on this food stuff. Of course, some people are lactose intolerant, and have problems processing dairy food, but the Toronto study has challenged the campaign against dairy, with some surprisingly edible results.

74 overweight adults undertook a 12-week study and were randomly assigned to one of three groups:

All the groups were counseled on healthy eating, so that they could manage their food intake. At the completion of the trial, the team took measurements including body weight, composition, cholesterol, blood markers, and metabolic health.

In both of the regular high fat dairy eating groups, the participants experienced improvements in their blood pressure while consuming a greater amount of protein, calcium, and vitamin D than the first group. Importantly, neither their waistlines nor BMI suffered. “Those that had three servings of dairy didn’t have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance,” explained Gerald Harvey Anderson, who was the lead author and works in the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto.”

With full-fat dairy containing more saturated fat than reduced fat products, how could this be? The experts believe that dairy’s combination of fats and protein is what makes it a positive food. “With dairy products, it’s got two proteins, casein and whey, that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in,” said Anderson. The “Dairy Matrix Hypothesis” suggests that the physical structure of dairy determines how the body processes its nutrient profile.

Of course, ice cream, milkshakes, and other treats that contain a ton saturated fat as well as massive amounts of sugar is a different story, but the Toronto study said its results with natural dairy products showed that  “Neither treatment nor time affected waist circumference, fat and fat-free mass, resting metabolic rate, fasting blood cholesterol, and urine creatinine.” The team concluded that “Frequent and daily consumption of full-fat dairy as part of a healthy diet is consistent with CFG (Canada’s Food Guide).”

This news also adds to another promising benefit of dairy, that was reported earlier this year. The American Academy of Neurology showed that those who regularly ate high fat cheese presented a 13% lower risk of dementia overall, and a 29% risk of vascular dementia. Cream was also associated with a 16% lower risk of all-type dementias.

The Toronto study found dairy to be a significant source of magnesium and potassium to boot. “The results align with the conclusion of an expert group that there is no evidence to support the avoidance of high-fat dairy in diets,” it said.

#8695. How to Correctly Add Forward and Reverse Lunges into Your Legday Workouts

When it comes to strengthening your legs, building muscles in your lower body, and improving all-round balance, lunges are a great move to lean into, but what is the difference between the forward and backward lunge? In a recent Instagram post, IFBB Pro, endurance athlete, and transformation coach Petar Klancir demonstrated the details.

Take a step in the right direction with these unique lunges.

“What is the difference?” asked The Croatian Colossus, who has built an Instagram base of more than one million followers thanks to his informative training videos. In essence, both of these variations are compound movements, so they tax multiple muscle groups at the same time. Whether you lunge forward or backward, you’ll be working the quads, hamstrings, calves and core. You will also flex the hips either way. But what does change is the emphasis placed on each muscle, and how they build your legs in different ways, as Klancir showed.

“Front step lunges target the quads more, due to the mechanics of the exercise,” explained Klancir. “The emphasis is on stepping forward, which requires the quads to control the impact of the foot’s landing. And there is a high degree of flexion.”

The quads take the majority of the load with forward lunges, because the mechanics that Klancir mentioned, require the quads to negotiate the lowering, and then lift your center of mass and return you to the starting position.

Tip: To avoid knee stress, be sure not to step out too far forward on the lunge. At the bottom of the lunge, your knee should only just be ahead of your chin.

“Back step lunges target the glutes and hamstrings,” said Klancir. “Due to emphasized hip-hinge movement.”

Reverse lunges are often considered easier to execute, because the front foot remains flat on the floor, providing a greater foundation and less requirement for core balance. They are also less stressful on the knee, because the load is shifted by the hamstrings and glutes to a greater extent than the quads.

Tip: Keep the front foot stable by keeping knee over ankle at all times.

For a complete leg blaster, your can try both movements by focusing on form. Then, once you are comfortable with your foot placings, you can build in some additional hypertrophy by adding a pair of dumbbells to the overall load.

Sam Retford, who is known to millions of Outlander: Blood of my Blood fans as Dougal MacKenzie, looks very comfortable on a show that requires him to navigate the unpredictable Scottish terrain, and there’s a good reason why. Not only does Retford love the great outdoors, but he’s also vastly experienced in a variety of skills. From riding a horse to cave diving, or rucking to offroad bike racing, this actor is as able as they come. So, staying still for just a second, Retford tells M&F why Outlander is such a personal and professional high, and how his favorite pastimes informed the role and his physique.

Now living in Glasgow, Retford’s love of adventure was passed down through blood. “My mum was a proper ranch cowgirl,” says Retford, who was born in Australia. “She has ridden horses all around the world, so she taught me to ride.” The star says that he loves nothing more than to get a bunch of pals together and go exploring, and has recently biked in The Himalayas, crossed the rivers of Amazonia, and cave dived around the United Kingdom. When the news came down that Retford would take up the role of Dougal MacKenzie and battle it out in 18th century Scotland, he was understandably all-in.

While most actors stay within the confines of a gym to ready for their roles, Retford added to his indoor workouts by acclimatizing to his new filming environment. As War Chieftain Dougal MacKenzie, Retford wanted to get a feel for the rugged highland landscape. “I wanted this guy to be physically capable,” he tells M&F, noting that he practiced rucking up and down the hills with a weighted backpack. “Even going and sleeping in the heather. I really wanted to build a physique capable of doing these long winter treks, but remain flexible enough to be agile in battle, to be strong enough to carry heavy loads—so everything had to be functional.”

The type of physique required to hunt and survive in the wilds of Scotland would not require a six-pack or be akin to an underwear model, so Retford wanted to build his character with authenticity. “I wanted him to have a big strong back and strong legs,” says the actor. “Okay, he can, lift but can he swing a sword around as well?”

Sam Retford earned a second-degree black belt in Taekwondo in his youth and understands the importance of exercise for agility and injury prevention. He also likes to swing the Indian Mace Bells for balance. But in the gym, his workouts include plyometric moves that require explosive power, such as box jumps. When lifting weights, the star focuses on time under tension and replicating proper form while squatting or making an overhead press.

The star also introduced instability into his lifting elements, for example with elevated platforms or unilateral movements in order to prepare him for the uneven ground outside. Still, the actor says that ultimately, the best way to prepare for his sprinting and fighting scenes was to run in the woods and climb trees. “Just moving about on set and staying warm,” he recalls.

Fans of Outlander: Blood of My Blood will have noticed that the physicality has leveled up in Season 2. For example, Dougal MacKenzie becomes embroiled in a serious battle in Episode 5 and must be rescued from being trapped underwater in Episode 6. Fortunately, the enthusiastic adventurer is more than comfortable with holding his breath. In Episode 2, Dougal also found himself in a fistfight with Brian Fraser (played by Jamie Roy).

Retford wants people to know, however, that progress is individual, takes time, and is not as easy as some social media accounts would like you to believe. He is also keen to point out that it takes a team of stunt coordinators, special effects wizards, lighting, and audio technicians to make any actor appear at their best. “You’ll notice I do quite a lot of shield work and headbutting, as opposed to sword fighting,” he explains. “That’s because I’m a lefty, and my right-handed combat is not very good. So, I have to keep the sword well and truly sheathed for a lot of it, to not cut anyone’s fingers off!”

Blood of My Blood no doubt the dream job for this thrill seeker. “Just to be out there in the cold, in the thick of it, running around, swinging swords. I mean, it’s a beautiful type of physicality, and it’s an amazing thing to call your job. So, I try never to complain. I’m always grateful.”

With Retford more than open to battling through a third season of Outlander: Blood of My Blood, the talented performer is also producing an upcoming documentary in Uganda and also has an eye on traveling to Mexico. “The key is to just say yes to crazy things,” he beams.

Season 2 of Outlander: Blood of My Blood premieres can be streamed via Starz.

When an American joins any branch of the United States military, they repeat an Oath of Enlistment to make the commitment official.

I do solemnly swear that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; and that I will obey the orders of the President of the United States and the orders of the officers appointed over me, according to regulations and the Uniform Code of Military Justice. So help me God.

On November 12, 2026, 64 men and women ventured to the Rayburn Office Building of the U.S. Capitol to take that oath and enter the Air Force and Space Force Delayed Entry Program. This swearing-in was the climactic moment of the second annual National Signing Day, an event hosted by the Air Force’s 317th Recruiting Squadron.

The concept of this event came from retired Air Force Master Sergeant and M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins, who said the idea was inspired by watching his son’s announcement for where he was going to play college football.

Wilkins explained, “I was watching this take place and thought to myself, ‘We should be doing something like this for the military.’”

Wilkins’ idea became a reality thanks to several people he worked with, including Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, Air Force Senior Master Sergeant Matt London, and others within the 317th. It made what was already a significant moment in the lives of these future service members even more memorable for them and their families who accompanied them.

Staff Sergeant Maddalyn Secrist was one of the recruiters on-hand for the event and was very involved with making the 2026 event a success. Secrist shared that having this on Capitol Hill took something local to the DMV area and gave it a sense of national awareness.

“It gives it more of a public view and gives these Airmen and Guardians the recognition that they need.”

Prior to their swearing-in, each person’s name was announced as they went to the table to sign on the dotted line and have their photo taken, reminiscent of the high school athletes who announce where they will play in college. Each new recruit was cheered by family, friends, and fellow American citizens as well as members of the Trump Administration like Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen B. Simmons and recently appointed Executive Director of the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition, Jacob Phillips.

Among those new recruits was Kevin McAllister, who was one of the older members of the group. At 35 years old and with a family tradition of service, McAllister knew that being physically prepared was a must, which is why he committed to longer runs and more intense training in preparation for the day. He also had to mentally dedicate himself to the process and suggests others who may be considering service do the same.

“I had to find the right mindset. There was a lot of running and calisthenics, but it taught me how to use different muscles,” he said. Even though he was fully prepared to take the oath, being in the Capitol definitely added a level of gravitas to the day.

“We are surrounded by the place where laws are made. The history of the United States is here. Just getting to add this to my family legacy makes me look at the flag differently.”

Bacon addressed the group and offered words of gratitude and encouragement that could be traced back to his own 30-year military career before entering the House of Representatives. He also shared wisdom that could be beneficial to people from all walks of life, whether they are in the military or not.

“Be the best at the job you’re going to get,” Bacon advised. “Learn that job inside and out so your boss can go, ‘I can trust that person.’”

There is no official word on future Signing Day events, but Secrist hopes that recruiters can use highlights or social media posts from this day to inspire their own applicants and create a similar experience to showcase why being a part of the Joint Force is so special.

Secrist said, “We think other recruiters can see this event and get inspired to do something like this in their own squadrons.”

To learn more about the Air Force or Space Force, go to airforce.com or spaceforce.mil.

#8679. JJ Spaun Got His Swing Back After a Misdiagnosis Nearly Wrecked His PGA Career

PGA star John Michael “JJ” Spaun has been at home with the golf clubs since he was gifted that first plastic toy set at age 3. But while the young protégé followed in his mother’s golf-playing footsteps, and furthered them by making progress in the PGA, a mysterious health issue would begin to derail his game.

Spaun sat down with M&F to discuss his initial Type 2 diabetes diagnosis, and how finally being discovered as Type 1 brought him back to greener pastures.

“I would say, in the majority, golf was a pretty easy sport for me to pick up,” says Spaun. “But I think I battled with what time and effort I wanted to put into it as a kid. Growing up in Southern California, other sports were pulling me in. Skateboarding was a huge presence at the time. I wanted to do what the other kids were doing culturally, which was skateboarding and extreme sports.”

In his youth, Spaun played a variety of sports aside from golf, including skateboarding, bicycling, baseball, basketball, and hockey. But while he did eventually fully embrace golf, his other experiences began to pay off. “I think those sports all played a role in my development, in my mechanics,” says Spaun. “Like hand-eye coordination, footwork. My swing coach, who I have been with for around six years, is a firm believer that skateboarding really developed my footwork for my golf swing even as a child. He considers my feet to be my superpower.”

JJ Spaun has just completed his 10th season with the PGA. He turned professional in 2012 and earned his first PGA Tour Card in 2016, but the players’ game began to take a downturn in 2018. He struggled with consistency and even lost his tour card during the 2020-21 season, where he placed 174th in the FedEx Cup rankings. Since the summer of 2018, Spaun found himself almost unable to complete a round of golf.

“I was 28 at the time,” he recalls. “I remember putting on my belt and running out of holes to put the notch in, so my belt was now too big for me. I suffered with severe thirst at night, and then frequently urinating, like, three or four times every night. I started losing weight very rapidly.”

Initially chalking all this up to a demanding golf season, Spaun decided to see a doctor after weighing himself and realizing that he’d inexplicably lost another 20 pounds in just a couple of months. The athlete was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes and hoped that the treatment would help him return to his prior form on the golf course. But that wasn’t to be.

“After three years, losing 50 pounds, going down to 155 pounds, I hadn’t weighed that since high school, so I finally got advice from an endocrinologist,” shares Spaun, who was then diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes, rather than Type 2.

Sadly, with 90% of diabetes sufferers having Type 2, medical advances for detecting Type 1 have been slower to emerge. Type 2 is often triggered by obesity, whereas Type 1 is thought to be more of a genetic issue causing the immune system to attack insulin producing cells in the pancreas. “They felt sorry for me, telling me that I was Type 1, but I said this is great, because I’ve been living miserably,” says Spaun. “My energy was at an all-time low. My golf was going down the drain. And now I had a real solution.”

Finally gaining the correct diagnosis in 2021, Spaun started insulin therapy. “In a matter of weeks, I could feel the strength coming back,” says the top golfer. “I was able to eat things without restricting my glucose range, as you do with Type 2. I started to feel better and things started coming together.”

Losing so much weight took time to overcome, however. “Your mechanics and your movements are off,” explains Spaun. “I’m glad to be handling things well. It’s definitely a challenge, but I’ve got all the support in the world to really make it as easy for me as possible.”

Incredibly, with the weight coming back and his treatment working well, Spaun had his breakthrough season in 2025, including a major victory at the 125th US Open. Spaun tells M&F that he uses a Dexcom G7 continuous glucose monitor to keep his levels in check and has recently switched from insulin injections to a pump system known as the Omnipod 5. “It’s been a game changer for me,” he shares.

In September 2026, Spaun was also able combine his love of traveling to England with his passion for golf, winning the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, and even donating a portion of his winnings to the Addington Fund, a British Charity that supports farming families. The golfer tells M&F that he discovered the financial hardships that many UK farms face during his holidays in the Cotswolds, where discovered the popular Prime series, Clarkson’s Farm.

“I’m the type of guy that likes to put in the work, because I’m a strong believer that you get out of this game what you put in,” says Spaun. But with the official season now over, the able athlete can look ahead to more family time, and another trip back to England.

No doubt, JJ Spaun is a highly decorated athlete with an even promising future, but living with diabetes has taught him that being present in the moment is more important than any trophy, so we conclude our interview and Spaun heads out on the school run.

#8677. What to Do About These High Interest Rates

Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?

Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.

Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.

Which brings up a few questions about whether we need to worry, or do anything about this new development.

These questions are on everybody’s mind these days, and I’ve been ruminating on them myself. But while I’ve seen a lot of play-by-play stories about each little interest rate increase in the financial newspapers, none of them seem to get into the important part, which is,

“Yeah, interest rates are way up, but what should I do about it?”

Why Is This Happening, and What Got Us Here?

Interest rates are like a giant gas pedal that revs the engine of our economy, with the polished black dress shoe of Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell pressed upon it.

For most of the past two decades, Jerome’s team and their predecessors have kept the pedal to the metal, firing a highly combustible stream of easy money into the system in the form of near-zero rates. This made mortgages more affordable, so everyone stretched to buy houses, which drove demand for existing homes and new construction alike.

It also had a similar effect on business investment: borrowed money and venture capital was cheap, so lots of entrepreneurs borrowed lots of money and started new companies. These companies then rented offices and built factories and hired employees – who circled back to buy more houses, cars, fridges, iPhones, and all the other luxurious amenities of modern life.

This was a great party and it led to lots of good things, because we had two decades of prosperity, growth, raising our children, inventing new things and all the other good stuff that happens in a successful rich country economy.

Until it went too far and we ended up with too much money chasing too few goods – especially houses. That led to a trend of unacceptably fast Inflation, which we already covered in a recent article.

So eventually, Jay-P noticed this and eased his foot back off of the Easy Money Gas Pedal. And of course when interest rates get jacked up, almost everything else in the economy slows down.

And that’s what is happening right now: mortgages are suddenly way more expensive, so people are putting off their plans to buy houses. Companies find that borrowing money is costly, so they are scaling back their plans to build new factories, and cutting back on their hiring. Facebook laid off 10,000 people and Amazon shed 27,000.

We even had a miniature banking crisis where some significant mid-sized banks folded and gave the financial world fears that a much bigger set of dominoes would fall.

All of these things sound kinda bad, and if you make the mistake of checking the news, you’ll see there is a big dumb battle raging as usual on every media outlet. Leftists, Right-wingers, and anarchists all have a different take on it:

The one thing all sides seem to agree on is that we are “experiencing hard economic times” and that “the country is headed in the wrong way”.

Which, ironically, is completely wrong as well – our unemployment rate has dropped to 50-year lows and the economy is at the absolute best it has ever been, a surprise to even the most grounded economists.

The reality? We’re just putting the lid back onto the ice cream carton until the economy can digest all the sugar it just wolfed down. This is normal, it happens every decade or two and it’s no big deal.

Okay, but should I take my money out of the stock market because it’s going to crash?

This answer never changes, so you’ll see it every time we talk about stock investing: Holy Shit NO!!!

The stock market always goes up in the long run, although with plenty of unpredictable bumps along the way. Since you can’t predict those bumps until after they happen, there is no point in trying to dance in and out of it.

But since we do have the benefit of hindsight, there are a few things that have changed slightly: From its peak at the beginning of 2022 until right now (August 2023 as I write this), the overall US market is down about 10%. Or to view it another way, it is roughly flat since June 2021, so we’ve seen two years with no gains aside from total dividends of about 3%.

Since the future is always the same, unknowable thing, this means I am about 10% more excited about buying my monthly slice of index funds today than I was at those peak prices.

Should I start putting money into savings accounts instead because they are paying 4.5%?

This is a slightly trickier question, because in theory we should invest in a logical, unbiased way into the thing with the highest expected return over time.

When interest rates were under 1%, this was an easy decision: stocks will always return far more than 1% over time – consider the fact that the annual dividend payments alone are 1.5%!

But there has to be some interest rate at which you’d be willing to stop buying stocks and prefer to just stash it into the stable, rewarding environment of a money market fund or long-term bonds or something else similar. Right now, if a reputable bank offered me, say, 12% I would probably just start loading up.

But remember that the stock market is also currently running a 10% off sale. When the market eventually reawakens and starts setting new highs (which it will someday), any shares I buy right now will be worth 10% more. And then will continue going up from there. Which quickly becomes an even bigger number than 12%.

In other words, the cheaper the stocks get, the more excited we should be about buying them rather than chasing high interest rates.

As you can see, there is no easy answer here, but I have taken a middle ground:

For most of us, the biggest thing that interest rates affect is our decisions around buying and selling houses. Financing a home with a mortgage is suddenly way more expensive, any potential rental house investments are suddenly far less profitable, and keeping our old house with a locked-in 3% mortgage is suddenly far more tempting.

Consider these shocking changes just over the past two years as typical rates have gone from about 3% to 7.5%.

Assuming a buyer comes up with the average 10% down payment:

This all sounds kind of bleak, but unfortunately it’s the way things are supposed to work – the tough medicine of higher interest rates is supposed to make the following things happen:

The net effect of all this is that prices should stop going up, and ideally fall back down in many areas.

This is a tricky one because the real “value” of a house depends entirely on supply and demand. The right price is whatever somebody is willing to pay for it. However, there are a few fundamentals which influence this price over the long run because they determine the supply of housing.

The first item (construction cost) is pretty interesting because it is subject to the magic of technological progress. Just as TVs and computers get cheaper over time, house components get cheaper too as things like computerized manufacturing and global trade make us more efficient.

I remember paying $600 for a fancy-at-the-time undermount sink and $400 for a faucet for my first kitchen remodel in the year 2001. Today, you can get a nicer sink on Amazon for about $250 and the faucet is a flat hundred. Similarly, nailguns and cordless tools and easy-to-install PEX plumbing make the process of building faster and easier than ever.

On the other hand, the last item (bullshit restrictions) has been very inflationary in recent times. I’ve noticed that every year another layer of red tape and complicated codes and onerous zoning and approval processes gets layered into the local book of rules, and as a result I just gave up on building new houses because it wasn’t worth the hassle. Other builders with more patience will continue to plow through the murk, but they will have less competition, fewer permits will be granted, and thus the shortage of housing will continue to grow, which raises prices on average.

Thankfully, every city is different and some have chosen to make it easier to build new houses rather than more difficult. Even better, places like Tempe Arizona are allowing good housing to be built around people rather than cars, which is even more affordable to construct.

But overall, since overall US house prices adjusted for inflation are just about at an all-time high, I think there’s a chance that they might ease back down another 25% (to 2020 levels). But who knows: my guess could prove totally wrong, or the “fall” could just come in the form of flat prices for a decade that don’t keep up with inflation, meaning that they just feel 25% cheaper relative to our higher future salaries.

The funny part about our current “high” interest rates is that they are not actually high at all. They’re right around average.So they might not go down at all for a long time.

Remember that graph at the beginning of this article? I deliberately cropped it to show only the years since 2009 – the long recent period of low interest rates. But if you zoom out to cover the last seventy years instead, you can see that we’re still in a very normal range.

But a better answer is this one: Interest rates will go down whenever Jerome Powell or one of his successors determines that our economy is slowing down too much and needs another hit from the gas pedal. In other words, whenever we start to slip into a genuine recession.

In order to do that however, we need to see low inflation, growing unemployment, and other signs of an economy that is finally cooling down. And right now, those things keep not showing up in the weekly economic data.

You can get one reasonable prediction of the future of interest rates by looking at something called the US Treasury Yield Curve. It typically looks like this:

What the graph is telling you is that as a lender you get a bigger reward in exchange for locking up your money for a longer time period. And way back in 2018, the people who make these loans expected that interest rates would average about 3.0 percent over the next 30 years.

Today, we have a very strange opposite yield curve:

If you want to lend money for a year or less, you’ll be rewarded with a juicy 5.4 percent interest rate. But for two years, the rate drops to 4.92%. And then ten-year bond pays only 4.05 percent.

This situation is weird, and it’s called an inverted yield curve. And what it means is that the buyers of bonds currently believe that interest rates will almost certainly drop in the future – starting a little over a year from now.

And if you recall our earlier discussion about why interest rates drop, this means that investors are forecasting an economic slowdown in the fairly near future. And their intuition in this department has been pretty good: an inverted yield curve like this has only happened 11 times in the past 75 years, and in ten of those cases it accurately predicted a recession.

So the short answer is: nobody really knows, but just for fun I’ll make a guess. Then if I’m wrong in public, you can come back and make fun of this in the comments.

I think we’ll probably see interest rates start to drop within 18-24 months, and the event may be accompanied by some sort of recession as well.

I like to read and write about all this stuff because I’m still a finance nerd at heart. But when it comes down to it, interest rates don’t really affect long-retired people like many of us MMM readers, because we are mostly done with borrowing. I like the simplicity of owning just one house and one car, mortgage-free.

With the current overheated housing market here in Colorado, I’m not tempted to even look at other properties, but someday that may change. And the great thing about having actual savings rather than just a high income that lets you qualify for a loan, is that you can be ready to pounce on a good deal on short notice.

Maybe the entire housing market will go on sale as we saw in the early 2010s, or perhaps just one perfect property in the mountains will come up at the right time. The point is that when you have enough cash to buy the thing you want, the interest rates that other people are charging don’t matter. It’s a nice position of strength instead of stress. And you can still decide to take out a mortgage if you do find the rates are worthwhile for your own goals.

So to tie a bow on this whole lesson: keep your lifestyle lean and happy and don’t lose too much sweat over today’s interest rates or house prices. They will probably both come down over time, but those things aren’t in your control. Much more important are your own choices about earning, saving, healthy living and where you choose to live.

With these big sails of your life properly in place and pulling you ahead, the smaller issues of interest rates and whatever else they write about in the financial news will gradually shrink down to become just ripples on the surface of the lake.

In the comments: what have you been thinking about interest rates recently? Have they changed your decisions, increased, or perhaps even decreased your stress levels around money and housing?

Well the first reason is that I’m not totally rational :-)

So like most of us, my decisions around money are made around what “feels” good, especially now that extra money doesn’t serve much purpose. It feels good pay off a margin loan that is at over 6%, and feels less good to see big interest bills coming in every month.

But if we’re talking about actually *selling* shares to move to another form of investment, the bar is much higher because you would owe full income tax (probably long-term capital gains tax) on the withdrawal.

Another reason is that 6% returns on a bank account are taxed as income while paying off 6% debt is after-tax. For a high earner, it’s closer to 9%.

Also, it has other advantages like freeing up additional cash flow because principal is also required when servicing that debt.

Mr. Money Mustache September 5, 2023, 2:56 pm

I’m usually in favor of at least 20%, because when you work out the effective interest rate increase that PMI is hitting you with, it usually works out to a very good return on that extra 10%.

For example, imagine a 500k house, and you are debating between a 50k or 100k downpayment (10 or 20%). And let’s say the interest rate is down at 5%.

If the PMI premium is a typical 0.8% of the loan value $450k, you’d be paying an extra $3600 per year in PMI premiums. Just for the privilege of not putting down the extra $50k.

That’s 7% of the potential extra downpayment that gets eaten up every year!

Or to put it another way, if you put in the second $50k, you are earning 5% in foregone loan interest PLUS 7% in saved PMI premiums. 12% in total, which is the best return around.

It’s a similar return when deciding between a 15 vs 30 year mortgage (the 15 year mortgage provides the extra risk free return). The return decreases the longer one keeps the mortgage, but for most people who move / re-finance within 7 years or so, it’s well worth it.

My brother got a mortgage from Navy Federal Credit Union with no PMI. So those deals are out there. This is not a VA loan, just standard mortgage. I’m thinking other credit unions might offer the same.

Essentially you “assume” the VA loan of another person instead of getting a new loan at today’s rates. The downside is that the purchase takes much longer, and since interest rates have been going down for decades, it hasn’t made sense to do an assumption loan for decades, so most people aren’t familiar with the process. We’re about 3 months into the process, and it’s looking like end-to-end it is going to take 5-6 months, but we’re assuming a 2.25% interest rate instead of today’s ~7%. You also can’t choose how much your down payment is. You have to have enough cash on hand to pay off whatever the difference is between the purchase price and what the seller has left on the mortgage.

My mortgage is 2.5% – P&I is $886/mo. Last year, we had about 28 years left and the interest was slightly higher than the principal payment each month – about $450/mo. or so in interest. Did a lump sum payment and cut off about 15 years of payments – now almost all my payment goes to the principal. The interest each month is now only about $230/mo.

In this sense, the savings in interest each month is about equal to what I’d be earning if I’d kept the lump sum in a money market. I’ve also got peace of mind because A. if I didn’t make another extra payment, I’ll still have a paid-for house in about 13 years, and B. since the money is already spent on the mortgage, it removes the temptation to find something else to use it on.

So the short answer to your comment is: yes, the front-loaded nature of the mortgage does factor into the equation. From an interest savings perspective, it’s definitely more profitable to pay the mortgage down during the first half of the amortization versus the last half.

As I understand it, the front-loaded nature of interest on a mortgage is just a reflection (the mirror image, maybe) of compound interest. So an extra principal payment in year 1 of a 30 year fixed-rate mortgage has a greater impact than one in year 25 because it has longer to compound, not because it gives a greater rate of return.

If you make an extra payment of $100 this year, next year your balance will be lower by $102.85. And in 27 years your balance will be lower by $100*1.0285^27=$213.56.

But if instead you put $100 in your high-yield savings account, next year you will have $105. So you really will approach the payoff amount faster that way (as long as the interest rate you’re earning remains higher).

You understand it correctly! You don’t pay more or less interest as a percentage of your loan by paying it off early or by paying it for 30 years – when you make extra payments early, you simply borrowed the total amount of money for less time. Naturally you pay less aggregate interest if you pay the loan off early, because you borrowed the total sum for less time. If your mortgage is 5%, for example, the total interest you pay as a percentage of what you borrowed will be 5% regardless of whether you pay off the loan in year 1 or year 30. Amortized payments confuse people into thinking that they’re paying more interest in the beginning than the end – no, you’re paying the percentage of whatever is outstanding. The amortization just allows one to have the same payment over the life of the loan, rather than a huge payment now and a itty bitty payment later. So it appears that you are paying more in interest, but it’s just that the interest that is owed is a greater percentage of the payment amount in the beginning because you owe more money.

In any case, you are totally correct that in a static situation paying yourself $100 into a 5% bank account instead of paying $100 extra to a 2.75% mortgage will earn you the delta (5-2.75 =2.25%) real annual return, compounded. Of course there’s no guarantee the savings return remains at 5%, whereas the interest rate on the fixed mortgage is guaranteed to be 2.75%.

Yeah, all good points – I didn’t mean to sound like a “just build more sprawl” type of person.

But I think that cities SHOULD open up the floodgates for infill redevelopment – stuff like the old parking lots and abandoned shopping malls that currently take up most of the space in central cities including mine.

But to stop the self-perpetuating problem of crowding and car traffic, make sure you have modern, people-friendly rules in place (which are also builder friendly because we’d rather build more houses rather than wasting land on car parking).

– eliminate “minimum parking” requirements – shrink roads and eliminate free taxpayer-paid car parking and make all the asphalt self-funding – add super safe and pleasant bike and pedestrian accomm0dation instead, which is more than 90% cheaper to build.

“Infill redevelopment” – I didn’t know there was a proper term for this but YES, that’s exactly what I’ve been saying for years. So much moaning & groaning over the “lack of affordable housing” – and yet, on the flip side, equal moaning & groaning over “strip mall ghost towns” and blighted areas of empty commercial properties. Instead of hacking up and parceling off more farmland and prairie to build overpriced McMansions with postage stamp-sized yards, why not develop what’s already there into housing? There are already all the roads, highways, byways, and parking lots you could ever need. Most also have some sort of parks or green space nearby, unkempt tho they may be, plus schools and access to public transportation. It seems like a no-brainer to me: instead of destroying more of what’s green and unsullied, why not rehab the bounty of concrete & steel & asphalt just sitting empty & unused?

I don’t pretend to understand all the reasons behind it, but I suspect it has more to do with a very few making a very large amount of money, than it does with anything truly prohibitive or “bad for humans” in trying to re-develop urban wastelands into habitable neighborhoods.

From what I’ve heard, commercial-to-residential conversions can be pretty complex, which is why you don’t see that many. The biggest challenges from what I hear are plumbing (offices/storefronts aren’t designed to have bathrooms/kitchens everywhere) and lack of windows (only on the outside, so interior spaces can’t be used as separate apartments). Not impossible, but often the retrofitting can wind up running more than just bulldozing the whole thing and starting from scratch. Starting with a parking lot might be easier.

Some developers are figuring out this puzzle, so hopefully the situation improves. There’s certainly plenty of unused commercial property to repurpose.

Bottom line is that it’s cheaper (for the developer) to build on fresh land in 95% of the cases. Redevelopment is far more expensive than new development. The costs for new development are often outsourced (new roads, new schools, new utilities, etc) whereas the developer is going to foot the bill on redevelopment (with some exceptions where a state/fed offers incentives for blighted areas, industrial waste sites, etc).

Attempting to control overpopulation is an unequivocally bad idea. A horrible scenario is going to play out in China in about a decade due to their one child policy. Most of the first world is heading for a situation of very problematic demographics (too many old people, not enough young). There is plenty of water even in a place like phoenix if it was priced and regulated appropriately, and we would have more than enough space in existing city boundaries if we didn’t subsidize parking and transportation in the worst ways possible. Changing those pricing and regulation schemes are the angles we need to look at, but we definitely need more units of housing.

I am based in Germany and snagged a historically low interest rate of .87% on my mortgage. The difference is that it is fixed for 10 years so this business of prediction is indeed quite critical to my short and mid term financial planning.

I have had the mindset of paying off the place as rapidly as possible just as a bit of a hedge on the long term uncertainty of life. I figure, worst case scenario with a paid off home I can ride off into the sunset. However, I like my job and see myself in my field at least another 20 years (I am 33). Hence, I have a bit of a challenge as interest rate predictions would seem to drive my behavior greatly: Option 1 – pay off a super low return mortgage to hedge a long term increasing rate Option 2 – pay off the minimum on my mortgage and invest the remainder because the delta is so massive due to the historic rate I snagged Option 3 – some hybrid of the two

There’s the option of an accelerated pay-off of my mortgage every year so I have until December to decide as I save throughout the year, but it is always interesting times as I do find I need to develop an opinion on the whole mortgage situation.

Option 2 makes the most sense to me. If you want to be conservative you can always invest the additional funds in some type of interest bearing account — in the US that would be something like FDIC insured CDs currently at over 5%, not sure what the German equivalent might be. Then, after 10 years you can use everything saved in the conservative interest bearing accounts and apply it to the mortgage all at once. You’ll have benefitted from the difference in interest rates.

Yes, the delta is massive, so take advantage of it if you have the discipline to not spend the money elsewhere!

There are ways to make it affordable; the question is if you’re willing to make it work.

A concrete example. I just bought a house in May 2023 at 6.75% interest and 5% down ($22k or so, which should be a cakewalk for most Mustachians), monthly payment of $3100. I have another house right down the street just like it that I converted into a duplex: 3br/1ba on both the first floor and basement (6br/2ba total). Those can both be rented out for $2200-2400 in my market as a standard rental, or for about $800/room if done by the room. So you could either live in one half for less than $1000/mo ($3100 – $2200 = $900), or live in one room and make a profit ($800 x 5 = $4000 – $3100 = +$900).

Does this take some work? Yes. Is it worth it for cheap/free/more than free living arrangements? I think so. And none of this is irreversible: you can kick people out or change the home layout once you pay the place off, increase income, or refinance into a more affordable payment.

Interest rates are like the weather, easy conversation with anybody but nothing you can really effect. And if it happens to you, it’s usually not tragic. For most people, excessive focus on interest rates can be distracting from more important decisions / choices.

There are areas of the USA that are frightfully expensive to live in … housing, taxes, transportation and even the need for private education because of failing schools.

For most people the more important decision is where you live and work and not the interest rate on your mortgage. For example, teacher in San Jose CA might make 15%-20% more than a teacher in East Cobb GA. But a home in San Jose will be close to 4x the price of a home in East Cobb. If you aren’t competing with high comp careers, you will have a nicer home earlier in your career and it will cost way less each month. Not everyone wants or can move across the country, but more should consider it. Even lesser distance choices like Sacramento show the difference in lifestyle potential. That $400k home in East Cobb at 8% w/20% down is about $3k/mo (15yr). That SJ $1.4mil home would be over $8k/mo even if the interest rate was half (4%). And the difference in down payment is huge. Life is easier and way less stressful if housing cost is zero. The path to zero is faster with lower cost housing in lower cost areas. For those who live on normal household incomes, where your home is might be way more important than any interest rate.

As far as investments go, if you are not an experienced financial professional or trader, interest rates are irrelevant. You can’t time interest rates or the market. The 80/20 rule (VTSAX/Bonds) rebalanced annually is the safest path for almost everyone. Anything else is really just a guess and sometimes a guess doesn’t work out well.

MMM, you have been a keen supporter of including REITs in your portfolio. However there are particular challenges for REITs in a rising interest rate environment. Would you advocate holding any existing allocation to REITs or reduce the holdings. Is there an optimum allocation to REITs? I have a 10% allocation and feel uncomfortable with this.

If you’re in REITs, beware of anything involving commercial property right now, including bigger multifamily housing. Unlike regular residential loans, these always wind up financed with ARMs with shorter terms, like 5-year or 7-year. With the rising rates, any of these forced to refinance in the current climate are likely to default or be much less profitable if they do survive. Some are forecasting GFC level crashes, this time on the commercial side as opposed to residential (which should be just fine).

Look at the Return on Assets the REIT (or any company) generates. Is this greater than or less than the interest they’ll have to pay to refinance their debts?

If they are earning less on their assets than it costs to finance the assets, expect losses or dividend cuts as they deleverage. E.g. they are borrowing at 6% to hold assets yielding 3%.

Lots of REITs with negative cash flows are in an unsustainable position. It would make sense for them to start shedding assets that no longer earn their cost of capital instead of burning cash while hoping for rates to fall. But when everyone does that…

Another misconception unrelated to your comment that is worth noting is that if the Fed cuts rates that the 10yr and mortgages will come down.  They will come down some but that is related to the option adjusted spread on the mortgage (don’t worry about what that part means, that’s maybe a 0.5%-0.75% swing factor).  Mortgages price off of longer dated treasury rates (~10yr treasury or blend of 5 and 10yr) and these are already baking in a series of cuts beginning in 2024.  So the cuts would need to be more significant than people expect to move mortgage rates significantly.  In other words, if the Fed cuts short term rates in an orderly fashion to 3.5% mortgages might not move all (aside from that option adjusted spread) and the yield curve might just look normal again.

#8675. How Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldowns Helped Jay Cutler Build an Even Wider Back

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Mass monster Jay Cutler, who claimed the title of Mr. Olympia on four occasions between 2006 and 2010, was never afraid to step away from the barbell if there was an efficient way to sculpt his back. Recently, the bodybuilder revealed that he liked to begin each back session with cable reverse-grip pulldowns. Here’s why.

“This was always the first exercise I started my back routine with,” confirmed Cutler in a recent video for his 5.7 million IG followers.

Techniques used by Jay Cutler to string together 25 consecutive top 2 finishes.

Utilizing a supinated (underhand) grip, you’ll primarily tax the lats while also recruiting the biceps and mid back. For many, the supinated grip is more comfortable on the shoulders than the pronated (overhand) grip. So, seated at the cable station, you’ll replicate a similar movement with the upper body to a chin up as you lower the bar. This grip also allows for heavier loads, making it perfect for adding upper body mass.

Tip: Keep your torso still and pull with the elbows until the bar is lowered just under your chin. Don’t pull any further down, or the load will shift to your forearms and shoulders.

“When you do something, reverse grip, it’s going to give you more flexion in those lats. It’s going to allow you to pull a little deeper and engage certain fibers,” explained Cutler who, as a competitive bodybuilder, was all about lifting heavy weights to create a winning physique.

In his video, Cutler kept the distance between his hands a little over shoulder width. “Pull down, focus on 12 repetitions,” he added. The Olympia icon also explained that the reverse grip lat pulldown was essential to building the winged appearance of his lats. “So, when I was doing that front double bicep (pose), it really yanked those lats out,” shared the legend. “And created that great V-taper.”

For Jay Cutler, the reverse grip lat pulldown was key to building muscle thickness. To try it for yourself, avoid using momentum and concentrate on the muscle contraction instead, as you lower the bar. Then slowly allow the bar to return skywards for additional time under tension.

#8664. Nick Walker Shares His Pre-Arnold Classic Upper-Body Workout

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Nick Walker is expected to hit the Arnold Classic stage in March, and if this heavy upper-body workout is anything to go by, “The Mutant” could be unstoppable in Columbus, OH, next year.

With the Arnold Classic now on his mind, the 2026 Mr. Olympia winner is hoping to top last year’s second place and rule this stage like he did last September at the Olympia. And, to get there, it appears that The Mutant is willing to push past his own superhuman limits. This was evidenced by a recent Instagram reel, in which Walker recorded a brutal but brilliant upper body session for his 2-million-plus followers.

With Olympia runner-up Samson Dauda speculated to enter, and Andrew Jacked confirming that he will try to defend his 2026 Arnold Classic trophy, Walker understands that each and every rep counts.

The 2026 Mr. Olympia found the ultimate success this time around with his outer sweep.

Walker’s video shows some seriously heavy sets, with the aim of reaching failure, so you should conduct some feeler sets to find the correct weight for you. For added safety, The Mutant is also spotted by IFBB Pro, Andy Paredes. “I’m not big on partners, but homie trains hard,” quipped Mr. Olympia in his IG caption.

The session started with the seated incline dumbbell press, a move that builds the shoulders, upper chest, and triceps. “Best chest on stage,” encouraged Paredes as Walker got ready to leave it all on the gym floor. “No weaknesses this year.”

Next up was the seated chest press machine, hitting the entire chest, shoulders, and triceps. Using the machine means that Walker can target these muscle groups effectively, while a traditional bench press requires the recruitment of the core for stabilization.

For his third exercise, The Mutant upped the anti with his chest dips, adding a plate suspended from his waist by a chain. And, if you are wondering what separates a chest dip from a triceps dip, it’s all about the positioning. Notice that Walker’s head and chest are forward, whereas triceps dips are characterized by a straighter torso. This way, the big man is activating the chest and anterior deltoids at the front of his shoulders

Moving on to the standing lateral raise machine, The Mutant turns his attention to the lateral (side) and rear deltoids, providing his upper body with a broader topline. Notice how he raises and then lowers the handles in a slow and controlled motion for added time under tension.

For his final exercise, Walker continues to build winning arms with standing barbell bicep curls, blasting those biceps and engaging the core to remain stable. Despite the heavy load, the 2026 Mr. Olympia once again concentrates on quality muscle contractions and time under tension.

To replicate these reps for yourself, aim for 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps on each exercise. The added weight on the chest dips is optional, but be sure to go heavy, taking in at least one feeler set to avoid injury. This may be a brutal workout, but the muscle building benefits could be brilliant.

#8660. 5 Pain-Free Arm-Building Alternatives to Barbell Curls

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The barbell biceps curl is arguably a cornerstone of arm day as well as a favorite among gymgoers.

But even with its popularity in the weightroom, there are subtle issues that could come from barbell curl, the main one being a straight bar could be uncomfortable for your wrists.

Unlike dumbbells, which offer more freedom of movement, the barbell doesn’t. That fixed grip might not vibe with your wrists and forearms as the weight gets heavier. With form issues like wrist hyperextension, questionable grip width, and a little too much body English, your wrists may rebel.

This doesn’t mean you should ditch it at the first sign of wrist discomfort. Sometimes, adjusting your grip, cleaning up your form, or checking your ego at the gym door is all that’s needed to start curling without wrist pain.

But sometimes, the barbell and your wrists will not get along.

Next, I’ll break down four common reasons barbell curls strain your wrists and what you can do about it. Then I’ll cover five biceps-building alternatives that let you pump up without the pain.

Here are four common reasons barbell curls bother your wrists and how to fix them.

Unlike dumbbells, a barbell locks both hands in a fixed position. Depending on your forearm anatomy, mobility, and grip width, this position may cause wrist discomfort. A barbell leaves little wiggle room, and your wrists may tell you all about it.

Quick Fix: Adjust your grip width for more comfort, or switch to a reverse grip.

As the load gets heavier or you become more fatigued, wrist hyperextension may happen. Instead of maintaining a wrist and forearm alignment, the bar pulls the hands backward. That adds extra demands on a body part that’s already working hard.

Quick Fix: Think knuckles in line with your forearms, and do a partial wrist curl to get your hands in that position.

There’s a time and place for body English, but if it causes unnecessary discomfort by pulling your wrist out of neutral during the curl, reconsider your strategy.

Quick Fix: Lighten the load, cut the set short when excessive momentum takes over, or use a three-second eccentric to slow things down.

Your forearms stabilize your wrists, and if you’ve already done a lot of grip work, your wrists may be tired before you begin. When your forearms and wrists fatigue, your grip may weaken, your wrist position may change, and your biceps will be left unsatisfied.

Quick Fix: If your grip gives out, do direct biceps work earlier in your workout with lighter loads, different grip positions, or the alternative exercises below.

If the form fixes didn’t work, it’s time for the alternative. A good alternative trains the biceps hard while addressing what made barbell curls uncomfortable in the first place.

Angled grips, neutral grips, and even overhand grips may feel better depending on your wrist and forearm anatomy. For example, an EZ bar reduces the amount of supination required, while hammer curls keep your palms facing each other.

Dumbbells, ropes, and resistance bands give your hands and wrists more freedom of movement than a barbell.

Look for exercises that keep your wrists neutral, let you control the lifting and lowering phases, and maintain biceps tension. Dumbbells, cables, and bands each feel different but may let you control the weight better without sacrificing gains.

The bottom line: A good barbell curl alternative should solve your wrist problem without creating a new one.

With that covered, here are five exercises that let you keep building bigger biceps without being married to the barbell.

Each exercise addresses one or more of the problems we discussed earlier, so choose wisely. Also, keep a mirror handy.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from the barbell’s fixed position.

The EZ-bar curl is the closest alternative to the barbell curl without locking the wrist in place. Its angled handles allow your forearms to sit in a slightly more neutral position, which many lifters find more comfortable than the barbell.

Form Tip: Choose a hand position that feels comfortable, and keep your wrists neutral.

Solves: Discomfort from the palms-up grip.

If you’ve been hammering the palms-up position, it’s time to switch. Using a palms-down grip shifts the exercise’s emphasis, placing greater demand on the brachioradialis and brachialis while the biceps still get the attention they deserve. The reverse curl provides a different stimulus and gives you another grip option if wrist pain is an issue.

Form Tip: Keep your elbows close to your sides, curl without body English, and lower with control.

Solves: The difficulty of keeping your wrists aligned during barbell curls.

The rope-cable hammer curl combines the wrist-friendly benefits of the dumbbell hammer curl with a touch of cable magic. This variation gives your wrists and hands more wiggle room, letting you adjust your hand spacing throughout the curl. The cable also provides constant resistance throughout the range of motion, enhancing biceps development.

Form Tip: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley and stand tall with your palms facing each other. Curl the rope toward your shoulders, then let your hands separate at lockout.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from a barbell’s fixed grip.

If barbell curls hurt your wrists, the answer may be to lighten the load and switch resistance types. That’s where the looped resistance band curl earns its place. Unlike a barbell, which provides the same external weight throughout the rep, a resistance band’s resistance increases as it stretches.

And don’t mistake bands for beginner-only equipment. Take a challenging set to near muscular failure with good form, and your biceps will thank you.

Form Tip: Grip the sides with your preferred grip, keep your wrists aligned, and curl toward your shoulders. Lower slowly without letting the band snap your hands back.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from limited freedom of movement.

Unlike a barbell, dumbbells let you rotate your forearms as you curl, moving from a neutral grip at the bottom to a palms-up position near lockout. This rotation is more joint-friendly while still engaging the biceps’ two primary functions: elbow flexion and forearm supination.

Form Tip: Start with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing inward. As you curl one dumbbell toward your shoulder, rotate your palm up. Squeeze your biceps at the top, lower under control, and repeat with the opposite arm.

Sets & Reps: 2–4 sets of 12-15 reps per side

Your biceps cannot tell the difference between a barbell, dumbbell, resistance band, or cable machine. They only care about tension. If that tension comes from a barbell and your wrists are annoyed, why keep hammering it when you have options?

If the form fixes above didn’t work, these five alternatives will help you train for gains without the pain.
